## NHRA Race Engineering Physics Laboratory

The established `nhra` command now also delegates ten additive race-engineering domains through the same authoritative NHRA facade: `nitro_powertrain_physics`, `multi_stage_clutch_lockup`, `tire_growth_wrinkle_shake`, `track_preparation_digital_twin`, `starting_line_bite_launch_envelope`, `christmas_tree_staging_physics`, `incremental_split_time_reconstruction`, `run_to_run_track_learning`, `nitro_engine_damage_parts_life`, and `between_round_turnaround`. `nhra capabilities` retains the original seven-domain championship/strategy inventory and exposes the new list under `race_engineering.domains`, preserving backward compatibility. Each domain accepts the same request/output/work-directory workflow used by the existing NHRA facade and emits deterministic evidence-digested reports.

These models are engineering simulation aids. They do not replace NHRA rulebooks, certified timing systems, manufacturer data, track-surface measurements, component inspection, or professional crew-chief judgment.


# Global UI Architecture and Engineering Shell

The global engineering shell extends the existing streamlined terminal without removing any command or option. It uses modular domain providers so vehicle, diagnostics, electronics, motorsport, safety, manufacturing, and research systems can register commands, forms, workflows, dashboards, issues, and contextual actions independently.

Objects in the current project are addressable using stable `muzix://` identifiers and appear in the Project Explorer. Selecting an object updates the persistent Inspector, adaptive home screen, contextual actions, search ranking, dashboard data, and workspace recommendation. Tabs and split layouts are persisted with the complete workspace state and restored after a terminal restart.

Forms accept rich values including physical quantities with units, ranges, object and artifact references, tables, expressions, matrices, and structured objects. Conditional fields remain available through full-schema disclosure. Every value records provenance such as project, workspace, preset, dataset, live source, derived calculation, user input, or command-line override.

Workflow definitions are directed graphs and can branch, validate, run parallel nodes, wait for conditions, request review, create checkpoints, and generate artifacts. Manual command sequences can be recorded and converted into reusable workflows. Long-running work appears in the unified job manager, while commands, state changes, issues, workflow steps, jobs, and artifacts appear in the activity timeline.

Dashboard layouts use a responsive grid and a rich widget library. Linked selection cross-filters related widgets. Large histories use virtualized paging; the terminal renderer updates changed cell spans only. The `ui performance` report exposes frame latency, input latency, changed spans, indexed objects, retained records, refresh rate, and throttling.

Accessibility narration can be minimal, standard, detailed, or diagnostic. Every rich widget requires a textual representation, and narrow or ASCII-only terminals receive compact sequential layouts rather than losing information.

Complete technical details and API examples are in `docs/GLOBAL_UI_ARCHITECTURE.md`.

# Chapter 63: Simulation Assurance, Resilience, and Reproducibility

## 63.1 Purpose, scope, and compatibility contract

The Simulation Assurance, Resilience, and Reproducibility (SARR) framework is the cross-cutting runtime that coordinates deterministic fault injection, transactional checkpoint/restart, structured error provenance, conservation closure, numerical-confidence evidence, dependency-aware result caching, and tamper-evident run certification. It is additive to the simulator. Existing vehicle models, diagnostics, motorsport platforms, project formats, scripts, plugins, APIs, checkpoint facilities, mathematical-assurance services, and command aliases remain available.

The command line remains the authoritative operator interface. The F7/Alt-M beginner menus are optional front ends that emit the same canonical `industrial assurance ...` commands handled by the normal dispatcher. A menu action does not invoke a separate assurance engine or bypass command validation, history, logging, or error handling.

The framework is intended to answer seven operational questions during a simulation or engineering campaign:

1. Can a failure be injected again in exactly the same place and sequence?
2. Can state be restored without leaving a partially recovered simulator?
3. Can an observed failure be traced to a stable error class and causal chain?
4. Do cross-subsystem conserved quantities close within explicit tolerances?
5. How trustworthy is a numerical result, and what evidence supports that trust classification?
6. Which results remain valid after a model, input, or dependency changes?
7. Can the resulting assurance state be sealed and verified as a reproducible run artifact?

The framework does not by itself establish regulatory approval, safety certification, homologation, or proof that a physical vehicle is safe. It provides engineering evidence and reproducibility controls that can support a qualified validation or certification process.

## 63.2 Architecture and runtime ownership

The public C++ entry point is:

```cpp
#include "aesim/assurance/resilience.hpp"

aesim::assurance::resilience::SimulationAssuranceFramework framework;
```

`AssurancePlatform` owns one framework instance. `IndustrialPlatform` connects the real industrial signal registry to the framework's hierarchical checkpoint tree and routes applicable production industrial commands through the deterministic fault guard. The resulting design uses one shared state model rather than independent demonstration subsystems.

The framework contains six cooperating services plus one orchestration surface:

| Service | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `DeterministicChaosEngine` | Reproducible fault rules, trigger evaluation, numeric corruption, delay/drop/failure decisions |
| `HierarchicalCheckpointManager` | Component registration, SHA-256 checkpoint identity, scoped restore, transactional rollback |
| `ErrorProvenanceGraph` | Stable error descriptors, runtime occurrences, causal links, state hashes, traces |
| `CrossSubsystemConservationLedger` | Dynamic conserved quantities, domain storage, external rates, transfers, closure verdicts |
| `NumericalEvidenceRegistry` | Numerical result provenance, uncertainty, residuals, conditioning, trust scoring |
| `SemanticResultCache` | Canonical semantic keys, dependency hashes, selective invalidation, incremental recomputation |
| `SimulationAssuranceFramework` | Unified status, production operation guards, manifests, certificates, and subsystem coordination |

The default checkpoint tree contains:

```text
assurance.errors
assurance.chaos
assurance.conservation
assurance.numerics
assurance.cache
industrial.signals
```

The first five are registered by the framework. `industrial.signals` is registered by the industrial platform and captures real simulator signal state.

## 63.3 Quick-start assurance workflow

A practical qualification session can begin with:

```text
industrial assurance framework status
industrial assurance checkpoint create clean-baseline
industrial assurance chaos seed 424242
industrial assurance conservation reset 0
```

After configuring faults, recording conservation state, and running the desired simulation, inspect and seal the evidence:

```text
industrial assurance error list
industrial assurance conservation status
industrial assurance numerics status
industrial assurance cache status
industrial assurance framework certificate run-certificate.json qualification-run
industrial assurance framework verify run-certificate.json
```

Before a destructive or high-risk fault campaign, create a checkpoint and verify it:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint create before-chaos
industrial assurance checkpoint list
industrial assurance checkpoint verify <checkpoint-id>
```

If the campaign leaves a state that should be discarded:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id>
```

A successful restore is transactional. If one restore callback fails after changing state, that component and all previously attempted components are rolled back in reverse order.

## 63.4 Deterministic fault-injection and chaos framework

### 63.4.1 Supported effects

The chaos engine supports the following effects:

| Effect | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `fail` | Raises a deterministic failure at the guarded operation |
| `exception` | Raises an explicitly injected exception |
| `delay` or `latency` | Adds a bounded delay; the current guard accepts `delay_ms` from 0 through 60000 |
| `drop` | Marks the guarded operation as dropped so it is not forwarded to the underlying subsystem |
| `corrupt` or `corruption` | Applies numeric corruption before the normal value-validation path |
| `resource-exhaustion` or `resource` | Injects the controlled resource-exhaustion failure path |

A triggered fault is also recorded as `ERR-ASSURANCE-FAULT` in the structured error graph.

Numeric corruption supports these modes in the C++/manifest interface:

| Mode | Result |
|---|---|
| `bias` | `value = value + configured_value` |
| `scale` | `value = value * configured_value` |
| `clamp` | Clamps to the configured `minimum` and `maximum` |
| `nan` | Replaces the numeric value with NaN |
| `inf` | Replaces the numeric value with positive infinity |

Corruption does not bypass the ordinary subsystem contract. For example, a corrupted industrial signal is still subjected to the normal signal validation rules. This is important because the framework tests the real production failure path rather than injecting an already-accepted final value.

### 63.4.2 Supported triggers

| Trigger | Alias | Activation rule |
|---|---|---|
| `invocation` | `count` | Fires when the matching subsystem/operation invocation count equals the configured count |
| `simulation-time` | `time` | Fires when the provided simulation time reaches or exceeds the configured threshold |
| `event` | - | Fires when the supplied event token exactly matches the configured event |
| `probability` | `probabilistic` | Uses the configured seed, rule identity, and invocation sequence to generate a deterministic probability decision |

Rules can target exact subsystem/operation names or use `*` wildcard fields. Rules are `once=true` by default; a once-only rule is added to the fired set after activation and does not fire again until reset or campaign replacement.

### 63.4.3 Deterministic replay

The default engine seed is fixed, and the operator can set an explicit 64-bit seed:

```text
industrial assurance chaos seed 424242
```

For probability rules, replay determinism depends on preserving the same:

- seed;
- rule identifiers and rule ordering;
- subsystem/operation matching sequence;
- invocation sequence;
- simulation-time/event context supplied to each evaluation.

Resetting the campaign resets the decision index, invocation counters, and fired-once set without deleting the rules:

```text
industrial assurance chaos reset
```

Deleting all rules and counters uses:

```text
industrial assurance chaos clear
```

### 63.4.4 CLI rule creation

Invocation-triggered failure:

```text
industrial assurance chaos add fail-third industrial.signal set fail invocation 3
```

Drop the first matching write:

```text
industrial assurance chaos add drop-first industrial.signal set drop invocation 1
```

Add a numeric bias to the first matching write:

```text
industrial assurance chaos add sensor-bias industrial.signal set corrupt invocation 1 bias 0.05
```

Add deterministic latency:

```text
industrial assurance chaos add delayed-read industrial.signal get delay invocation 2 25
```

Trigger evaluation without executing a production command:

```text
industrial assurance chaos trigger industrial.signal set 12.5 calibration-event
```

The `trigger` form reports activated decisions and records them in the error graph. It is useful for checking a campaign before applying it to a real operation.

### 63.4.5 Fault manifests and transactional loading

A campaign can be stored in a JSON/YAML document accepted by the project document parser. A representative JSON form is:

```json
{
  "seed": 424242,
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "drop-third-write",
      "subsystem": "industrial.signal",
      "operation": "set",
      "effect": "drop",
      "trigger": "invocation",
      "invocation": 3,
      "once": true,
      "enabled": true,
      "parameters": {}
    },
    {
      "id": "bias-first-write",
      "subsystem": "industrial.signal",
      "operation": "set",
      "effect": "corrupt",
      "trigger": "invocation",
      "invocation": 1,
      "once": true,
      "enabled": true,
      "parameters": {
        "mode": "bias",
        "value": 0.05
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Load it with:

```text
industrial assurance chaos load campaign.json
```

Loading is transactional with respect to validation. The complete manifest is parsed and validated before its rules are committed. Invalid rule IDs, duplicate IDs, invalid trigger/effect parameters, malformed delay/corruption contracts, or an invalid root structure are rejected instead of partially replacing the active campaign.

### 63.4.6 Recovery access during a chaos campaign

Assurance control commands are intentionally outside the production-operation fault guard. This prevents a fault campaign from blocking the operator's ability to inspect faults, remove rules, restore checkpoints, or verify evidence.

Useful recovery commands are:

```text
industrial assurance chaos status
industrial assurance chaos remove <rule-id>
industrial assurance chaos clear
industrial assurance checkpoint list
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id>
industrial assurance error list
```

## 63.5 Hierarchical checkpoint/restart with transactional recovery

### 63.5.1 Checkpoint identity and contents

Each checkpoint stores:

- checkpoint ID;
- human-readable label;
- UTC creation timestamp;
- optional parent checkpoint ID;
- component state documents;
- SHA-256 digest for every component;
- aggregate SHA-256 digest;
- optional metadata.

Create a checkpoint:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint create pre-test
```

Create a checkpoint associated with an existing parent checkpoint:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint create after-calibration <parent-checkpoint-id>
```

The parent relationship records lineage. It does not imply that unchanged component data can be omitted from the current checkpoint.

### 63.5.2 Verification and persistence

List/check status:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint status
industrial assurance checkpoint list
```

Verify an in-memory checkpoint:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint verify <checkpoint-id>
```

Persist it:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint save <checkpoint-id> checkpoint.json
```

Load a persisted checkpoint back into the manager:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint load checkpoint.json
```

A checkpoint is not trusted merely because it parses. Verification checks the stored component identities and aggregate identity against the actual checkpoint content.

### 63.5.3 Hierarchical scoped restore

Restore all checkpoint components:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id>
```

Restore one exact component:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id> assurance.chaos
```

Restore a hierarchy:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id> assurance
```

The `assurance` scope applies all checkpoint components whose paths fall under the assurance hierarchy. `industrial.signals` can be restored independently when only signal state should be recovered.

### 63.5.4 Transactional restore semantics

The manager performs a recoverable restore using this sequence:

1. Identify the checkpoint components included by the requested scope.
2. Capture the current pre-restore state of every affected component.
3. Order components deterministically using their restore ordering.
4. Mark each component as rollback-eligible before invoking its restore callback.
5. Apply checkpoint state.
6. If any callback fails, restore the failing component and every previously attempted component in reverse order.
7. Return a `RestoreReport` describing success, rollback attempt, rollback result, restored component count, scope, checkpoint ID, and error text.

This guards against the difficult case in which a component mutates state and then throws. The failing component itself is included in rollback, rather than only components completed before it.

If restore fails and rollback also fails, the framework records `ERR-ASSURANCE-RECOVERY`, whose default severity is `CRITICAL` and whose default descriptor is non-recoverable. Preserve incident evidence and restart from a separately verified checkpoint rather than assuming the process state is clean.

## 63.6 Structured error taxonomy and failure provenance graph

### 63.6.1 Error descriptors

A descriptor defines the stable meaning of an error code:

- code;
- category;
- severity;
- title;
- description;
- recoverable flag;
- remediation actions.

Default framework descriptors are:

| Code | Severity | Meaning | Recoverable default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ERR-ASSURANCE-FAULT` | WARNING | A deterministic fault rule activated | Yes |
| `ERR-ASSURANCE-CONSERVATION` | ERROR | Conservation closure exceeded tolerance | Yes |
| `ERR-ASSURANCE-NUMERICAL` | ERROR | Numerical result failed trust requirements | Yes |
| `ERR-ASSURANCE-RECOVERY` | CRITICAL | Transactional checkpoint recovery failed | No |

Inspect the catalog:

```text
industrial assurance error catalog
```

### 63.6.2 Runtime occurrences

Each occurrence records:

- monotonic occurrence ID;
- taxonomy code;
- UTC timestamp;
- subsystem;
- operation;
- human-readable message;
- zero or more causal occurrence IDs;
- structured context;
- optional simulator-state SHA-256.

List current occurrences:

```text
industrial assurance error list
```

Manually add an occurrence using a registered code:

```text
industrial assurance error record ERR-ASSURANCE-FAULT operator test manual-event
```

Clear runtime occurrences without deleting the descriptor catalog:

```text
industrial assurance error clear
```

### 63.6.3 Causal provenance

An occurrence may reference earlier occurrences as causes. Invalid or nonexistent causal IDs are rejected. Restored graph state is validated so malformed ordering or IDs do not silently enter the graph.

Trace an occurrence:

```text
industrial assurance error trace <occurrence-id>
```

The trace is intended to answer not only "what failed?" but also "which earlier failure evidence led to this occurrence?". For postmortem work, save the related checkpoint and run certificate alongside the error trace so the causal graph can be correlated with exact simulator state.

## 63.7 Cross-subsystem conservation ledger

### 63.7.1 Default conserved quantities

The framework defines these quantities at construction time:

| Quantity | Unit | Absolute tolerance | Relative tolerance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `energy` | J | 1.0 | 1e-6 |
| `mass` | kg | 1e-8 | 1e-7 |
| `charge` | C | 1e-6 | 1e-7 |
| `linear_momentum` | kg*m/s | 1e-5 | 1e-6 |
| `angular_momentum` | kg*m^2/s | 1e-5 | 1e-6 |

Additional quantities can be defined explicitly:

```text
industrial assurance conservation define refrigerant_mass kg 1e-8 1e-7
```

### 63.7.2 State, external rates, and transfers

Start a ledger interval:

```text
industrial assurance conservation reset 0
```

Initialize stored quantities before adding their rates:

```text
industrial assurance conservation storage engine energy 100000
industrial assurance conservation storage battery energy 0
```

Record an external signed rate:

```text
industrial assurance conservation external engine energy 500
```

Record a transfer between two domains once:

```text
industrial assurance conservation transfer engine battery energy 1000
```

The transfer is applied with opposite sign to the source and destination domain. It should not be entered twice.

Update storage at the end of the interval and close the step:

```text
industrial assurance conservation storage engine energy 99000
industrial assurance conservation storage battery energy 1000
industrial assurance conservation close 1
```

### 63.7.3 Closure calculation and interpretation

For each initialized domain/quantity cell, the ledger computes:

```text
storage_change = current_storage - previous_storage
external_net   = dt * external_rate
transfer_net   = dt * transfer_rate
residual       = storage_change - external_net - transfer_net
```

The residual is normalized by an absolute-plus-relative tolerance scale. A normalized residual less than or equal to 1 passes. A nonfinite normalized residual fails. Any failing cell makes the overall step fail and records `ERR-ASSURANCE-CONSERVATION` when the step is closed through the CLI.

Rates cannot be entered for a domain/quantity cell until storage has been initialized. This prevents an omitted storage state from silently disappearing from the balance.

After `close`, the current storage becomes the next interval's previous storage and accumulated external/transfer rates are cleared.

### 63.7.4 Example interpretation

A report can resemble:

```text
Conservation step=4 interval=[3,4] verdict=FAIL violations=1
PASS battery.energy residual=0 J normalized=0
FAIL engine.energy residual=2.5 J normalized=1.42
```

A failure should lead to inspection of model coupling, sign conventions, unit consistency, solver error, missed storage terms, and the timing used for integrated rates. Increasing tolerances should not be the first response unless the existing tolerance is demonstrably inconsistent with the model's validated error budget.

## 63.8 Numerical provenance and confidence-aware results

### 63.8.1 Evidence fields

A `NumericalEvidence` record can carry:

- stable/deterministic evidence ID;
- metric name;
- numeric value and unit;
- absolute uncertainty;
- confidence level;
- algorithm and solver identity;
- precision in bits;
- residual and tolerance;
- condition estimate;
- iteration count;
- convergence flag;
- model-validity-domain flag;
- provenance links;
- input SHA-256;
- result SHA-256;
- UTC timestamp;
- derived trust score and trust class.

Record basic evidence from the CLI:

```text
industrial assurance numerics record brake-temp brake_temperature 800 degC 0.1 0.99 BDF 1e-10 1e-6 20 53
```

Use `-` as the ID to allow the registry to derive a deterministic ID from the metric and available SHA-256 material:

```text
industrial assurance numerics record - brake_temperature 800 degC 0.1 0.99 BDF 1e-10 1e-6 20 53
```

Inspect one result:

```text
industrial assurance numerics get <evidence-id>
```

Inspect all evidence:

```text
industrial assurance numerics status
industrial assurance numerics list
```

Export the current registry atomically:

```text
industrial assurance numerics export numerical-evidence.json
```

### 63.8.2 Evidence validation

The registry rejects invalid contracts rather than merely assigning them a poor score. Invalid examples include:

- nonfinite result value, uncertainty, residual, tolerance, or condition estimate;
- negative uncertainty;
- negative tolerance;
- negative condition estimate;
- confidence outside `[0,1]`;
- impossible precision-bit values;
- malformed SHA-256 identities where a hash is supplied.

The runtime also rejects a result through the trust model when it is nonconverged or outside its declared model-validity domain. A rejected numerical result is recorded in the error graph as `ERR-ASSURANCE-NUMERICAL` when entered through the CLI.

### 63.8.3 Trust score

The current trust score is a bounded value in `[0,1]`. It begins at 1 and is reduced by factors representing relative uncertainty, residual relative to tolerance, high condition estimate, reduced precision, and confidence below 0.95. Nonfinite, nonconverged, or out-of-domain results receive zero trust.

Trust classes are:

| Trust score | Class |
|---:|---|
| `>= 0.85` | `HIGH` |
| `>= 0.60` and `< 0.85` | `MEDIUM` |
| `>= 0.30` and `< 0.60` | `LOW` |
| `< 0.30` | `REJECT` |

A `HIGH` classification is not a replacement for model validation. It means the evidence record satisfies the current numerical trust policy; it does not prove that the underlying physical model is correct.

## 63.9 Semantic result caching and incremental recalculation

### 63.9.1 Semantic cache identity

A result is keyed by:

- namespace;
- canonical input-document SHA-256;
- canonical settings-document SHA-256;
- sorted named dependency hashes.

This makes cache validity depend on engineering meaning rather than only a filename or opaque object address.

Set a dependency semantic hash:

```text
industrial assurance cache dependency vehicle.model model-v1
```

Store a result using JSON text or readable document files:

```text
industrial assurance cache put lap-time inputs.json settings.json result.json vehicle.model baseline
```

The optional dependencies and tags are comma-separated. Use `-` where an optional set should be empty.

### 63.9.2 Cache lookup

Retrieve by semantic key:

```text
industrial assurance cache get <key>
```

The CLI reports one of:

```text
cache HIT
cache STALE
cache MISS
```

The C++ `get_or_compute` path provides incremental recalculation. An unchanged semantic key returns the stored result and does not invoke the supplied compute function. A miss or invalidation invokes the computation and stores the resulting value.

### 63.9.3 Dependency-aware invalidation

Updating a dependency invalidates only entries that explicitly reference that dependency:

```text
industrial assurance cache dependency vehicle.model model-v2
```

Explicit invalidation is also available:

```text
industrial assurance cache invalidate dependency vehicle.model
industrial assurance cache invalidate tag baseline
industrial assurance cache invalidate namespace lap-time
```

Clear all cache entries:

```text
industrial assurance cache clear
```

### 63.9.4 Persistence and integrity

Persist the cache atomically:

```text
industrial assurance cache save semantic-cache.json
```

Restore it:

```text
industrial assurance cache load semantic-cache.json
```

A restored cache is validated before acceptance. Every entry's dependency hashes must match the dependency registry, and the semantic key is recomputed from the namespace/input/settings/dependency identity. A stale dependency or key mismatch causes load rejection instead of silently serving the stored result.

Status reports include entry count, dependency count, hits, misses, hit rate, and invalidation count:

```text
industrial assurance cache status
```

## 63.10 Reproducibility manifests and tamper-evident certificates

### 63.10.1 Manifest contents

`SimulationAssuranceFramework::manifest()` produces schema:

```text
aesim.simulation-assurance-resilience-reproducibility.v1
```

The manifest includes:

- schema/version;
- UTC creation timestamp;
- run name;
- chaos-engine state;
- error taxonomy and occurrence graph;
- checkpoint index;
- conservation state;
- numerical-evidence registry;
- semantic-cache state;
- canonical content SHA-256.

Create a certificate:

```text
industrial assurance framework certificate run-certificate.json qualification-run
```

`manifest` is accepted as an alias for `certificate`:

```text
industrial assurance framework manifest run-certificate.json qualification-run
```

Verify it:

```text
industrial assurance framework verify run-certificate.json
```

### 63.10.2 Canonical verification semantics

Verification parses the document, checks the expected schema, removes the stored `content_sha256`, canonicalizes the remaining JSON semantics, recomputes SHA-256, and compares it with the stored digest.

Consequences:

- semantic content tampering fails verification;
- changing authenticated values fails verification;
- deleting the digest fails verification;
- changing only insignificant JSON formatting/whitespace does not fail verification because raw byte formatting is not the authenticated object.

A certificate proves integrity of the included assurance manifest. It does not cryptographically authenticate a person's identity unless a separate signature/trust process is applied outside this SHA-256 content seal.

## 63.11 Integrated framework status

The following commands are equivalent framework-status entry points:

```text
industrial assurance framework status
industrial assurance resilience status
industrial assurance sar status
industrial assurance reproducibility status
```

The combined report contains:

- deterministic chaos seed, rule count, and decision count;
- checkpoint inventory/report;
- error catalog/occurrence status;
- conservation quantities/domains/last closure;
- numerical evidence status;
- semantic cache statistics.

Use this command at the beginning and end of a qualification session so run logs record the active assurance state.

## 63.12 Complete CLI command reference

The canonical command family is `industrial assurance`. Several area aliases exist, but scripts should prefer the canonical spelling for readability.

### 63.12.1 Framework

```text
industrial assurance framework status
industrial assurance framework certificate <path> [run-name]
industrial assurance framework manifest <path> [run-name]
industrial assurance framework verify <path>
```

Aliases for the `framework` area are `sar`, `resilience`, and `reproducibility`.

### 63.12.2 Chaos/fault injection

```text
industrial assurance chaos status
industrial assurance chaos list
industrial assurance chaos seed <unsigned-64-bit-seed>
industrial assurance chaos load <manifest-file>
industrial assurance chaos clear
industrial assurance chaos reset
industrial assurance chaos remove <rule-id>
industrial assurance chaos add <id> <subsystem> <operation> <effect> <trigger> <value> [effect-parameters...]
industrial assurance chaos trigger <subsystem> <operation> [simulation-time-s] [event]
```

Aliases for `chaos` are `fault` and `faults`.

For `corrupt` through the CLI, append the corruption mode and value:

```text
... corrupt invocation 1 bias 0.05
... corrupt invocation 1 scale 1.02
```

For `delay`, append delay milliseconds:

```text
... delay invocation 1 50
```

For richer corruption settings such as `clamp`, `nan`, or `inf`, use a campaign manifest or the C++ API so the complete parameter object can be supplied.

### 63.12.3 Checkpoints

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint status
industrial assurance checkpoint list
industrial assurance checkpoint create <label> [parent-id]
industrial assurance checkpoint save <id> <path>
industrial assurance checkpoint load <path>
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <id> [scope]
industrial assurance checkpoint verify <id>
```

`checkpoints` is accepted as an area alias.

### 63.12.4 Error taxonomy/provenance

```text
industrial assurance error status
industrial assurance error catalog
industrial assurance error list
industrial assurance error trace <occurrence-id>
industrial assurance error record <code> <subsystem> <operation> <message...>
industrial assurance error clear
```

`errors` is accepted as an area alias.

### 63.12.5 Conservation ledger

```text
industrial assurance conservation status
industrial assurance conservation reset [time-s]
industrial assurance conservation define <quantity> <unit> <absolute-tolerance> <relative-tolerance>
industrial assurance conservation storage <domain> <quantity> <value>
industrial assurance conservation external <domain> <quantity> <rate>
industrial assurance conservation transfer <from-domain> <to-domain> <quantity> <rate>
industrial assurance conservation close <time-s>
```

`ledger` is accepted as an area alias.

### 63.12.6 Numerical evidence

```text
industrial assurance numerics status
industrial assurance numerics list
industrial assurance numerics record <id-or-dash> <metric> <value> <unit> <uncertainty> <confidence> <solver> <residual> <tolerance> <condition-estimate> [precision-bits]
industrial assurance numerics get <id>
industrial assurance numerics clear
industrial assurance numerics export <path>
```

`numerical` is accepted as an area alias.

### 63.12.7 Semantic cache

```text
industrial assurance cache status
industrial assurance cache dependency <name> <semantic-hash>
industrial assurance cache put <namespace> <inputs-json-or-file> <settings-json-or-file> <value-json-or-file> [dependencies-csv] [tags-csv]
industrial assurance cache get <key>
industrial assurance cache invalidate dependency <name>
industrial assurance cache invalidate tag <tag>
industrial assurance cache invalidate namespace <namespace>
industrial assurance cache clear
industrial assurance cache save <path>
industrial assurance cache load <path>
```

JSON arguments can be inline JSON or paths to readable document files. A malformed file or string that is neither valid JSON nor a readable document is rejected.

## 63.13 Beginner-menu integration without removing the command line

Press:

```text
F7
```

or:

```text
Alt-M
```

The beginner menus expose assurance entry points under Analyze and Validate. Current menu actions include:

- Numerical confidence;
- Conservation ledger;
- Assurance health;
- Recovery checkpoints;
- Fault injection status.

The menu is a command generator. It does not replace the prompt.

- `Enter` executes the displayed canonical command through the normal CLI dispatcher.
- `Tab` inserts the displayed command into the persistent command line so it can be inspected or edited first.
- `Esc` closes the menu and returns to the existing workspace.

Experienced operators can ignore the menus entirely and use only `industrial assurance ...` commands.

## 63.14 Worked workflow: deterministic industrial-signal fault and recovery

This workflow demonstrates the relationship among checkpointing, fault injection, error provenance, and recovery.

1. Inspect the framework:

```text
industrial assurance framework status
```

2. Create a baseline checkpoint:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint create before-signal-fault
```

3. Add a deterministic first-write drop:

```text
industrial assurance chaos add drop-signal industrial.signal set drop invocation 1
```

4. Run the normal industrial signal write command used by the current project. The guard evaluates the fault rule before forwarding the production command.

5. Inspect the campaign and error graph:

```text
industrial assurance chaos status
industrial assurance error list
```

6. Trace the fault occurrence if required:

```text
industrial assurance error trace <occurrence-id>
```

7. Restore the real signal state from the checkpoint:

```text
industrial assurance checkpoint restore <checkpoint-id> industrial.signals
```

8. Remove the rule and verify recovery status:

```text
industrial assurance chaos remove drop-signal
industrial assurance framework status
```

The important property is that the signal registry participating in the checkpoint is the actual industrial signal state, not a demonstration copy.

## 63.15 Worked workflow: conservation and numerical evidence

A simple cross-domain energy study can be recorded as:

```text
industrial assurance conservation reset 0
industrial assurance conservation storage engine energy 100000
industrial assurance conservation storage battery energy 0
industrial assurance conservation transfer engine battery energy 1000
industrial assurance conservation storage engine energy 99000
industrial assurance conservation storage battery energy 1000
industrial assurance conservation close 1
```

If a solver-derived brake temperature is also part of the run:

```text
industrial assurance numerics record brake-temp brake_temperature 800 degC 0.1 0.99 BDF 1e-10 1e-6 20 53
industrial assurance numerics get brake-temp
```

Before accepting the run, inspect both sources of evidence:

```text
industrial assurance conservation status
industrial assurance numerics status
industrial assurance error list
```

Then seal them with the rest of the assurance state:

```text
industrial assurance framework certificate evidence/run.json brake-energy-study
industrial assurance framework verify evidence/run.json
```

## 63.16 Worked workflow: dependency-aware recalculation

Assume a lap-time result depends on `vehicle.model` and `tire.model`.

1. Establish semantic dependency versions/hashes:

```text
industrial assurance cache dependency vehicle.model model-v1
industrial assurance cache dependency tire.model tire-v7
```

2. Store a result:

```text
industrial assurance cache put lap-time inputs.json settings.json result.json vehicle.model,tire.model baseline
```

3. Record the returned cache key.

4. Retrieve the result:

```text
industrial assurance cache get <key>
```

5. Change only the tire dependency:

```text
industrial assurance cache dependency tire.model tire-v8
```

Only entries declaring `tire.model` are invalidated. Entries depending only on `vehicle.model` remain available.

6. In C++, call `get_or_compute`. The compute callback is invoked only when the semantic lookup cannot reuse a valid entry.

This mechanism is suitable for expensive engineering studies because it avoids treating every project change as a reason to recompute unrelated results.

## 63.17 C++ integration examples

### 63.17.1 Register a checkpoint component

```cpp
using namespace aesim::assurance::resilience;

framework.checkpoints().register_component({
    "vehicle.custom_state",
    60,
    [&] {
        return capture_custom_state();
    },
    [&](const aesim::doc::Value& value) {
        restore_custom_state(value);
    }
});
```

Capture and restore callbacks must represent the complete state required for deterministic recovery of that component. A restore callback should throw on invalid input rather than silently applying a partial state.

### 63.17.2 Guard a production operation

```cpp
FaultContext context;
context.subsystem = "vehicle.custom";
context.operation = "update";
context.simulation_time_s = simulation_time_s;
context.event = current_event;

const auto guard = framework.guard(context);
if (!guard.dropped) {
    perform_update();
}
```

If the guarded value is numeric, apply corruption decisions before the subsystem's normal validation:

```cpp
const double injected = framework.chaos().apply_numeric(raw_value, guard.decisions);
validate_and_apply(injected);
```

### 63.17.3 Cache expensive work

```cpp
const auto lookup = framework.cache().get_or_compute(
    "lap-time",
    input_document,
    settings_document,
    [&] { return run_expensive_lap_simulation(); },
    {"baseline"},
    {"vehicle.model", "tire.model"});
```

`lookup.recomputed` distinguishes a newly calculated result from a reused cache entry.

### 63.17.4 Record numerical evidence

```cpp
NumericalEvidence evidence;
evidence.metric = "brake_temperature";
evidence.value = 800.0;
evidence.unit = "degC";
evidence.absolute_uncertainty = 0.1;
evidence.confidence_level = 0.99;
evidence.algorithm = "BDF";
evidence.solver = "BDF";
evidence.precision_bits = 53;
evidence.residual = 1.0e-10;
evidence.tolerance = 1.0e-6;
evidence.condition_estimate = 20.0;
evidence.converged = true;
evidence.inside_validity_domain = true;
framework.numerics().record(std::move(evidence));
```

## 63.18 Persistence schemas and integrity boundaries

The framework uses explicit schema identifiers for persisted subsystem state:

```text
aesim.deterministic-chaos.v1
aesim.conservation-ledger.v1
aesim.numerical-evidence.v1
aesim.semantic-cache.v1
aesim.simulation-assurance-resilience-reproducibility.v1
```

Checkpoint files also contain checkpoint identity and per-component/aggregate SHA-256 evidence. Cache restore validates dependency coherence and recomputes semantic keys. Chaos restore validates rule identities, trigger/effect contracts, invocation counters, and fired-rule references. Numerical-evidence restore validates precision, finite values, trust-related fields, and supplied hashes.

Persistence failures should be treated as evidence failures, not ignored warnings. Keep the original artifact when investigating a rejected document; do not edit it in place and then attempt to prove the original run.

## 63.19 Error handling and recovery guidance

Use the following response hierarchy:

### Deterministic injected fault

```text
industrial assurance error list
industrial assurance chaos status
industrial assurance chaos remove <rule-id>
```

Restore a checkpoint if the operation changed persistent simulator state before another downstream failure occurred.

### Conservation violation

```text
industrial assurance conservation status
industrial assurance error list
```

Inspect sign conventions, storage initialization, transfer duplication, units, step timing, and solver accuracy before widening tolerances.

### Low-trust numerical result

```text
industrial assurance numerics get <id>
industrial assurance error list
```

Inspect residual/tolerance ratio, condition estimate, precision, uncertainty, convergence, and model-validity status. Consider higher precision or an independent solver/reference calculation when the evidence indicates conditioning or convergence risk.

### Checkpoint verification failure

Do not restore an unverified checkpoint merely because its JSON parses. Preserve the artifact for postmortem analysis and use another verified checkpoint.

### Transactional recovery failure

`ERR-ASSURANCE-RECOVERY` is critical and non-recoverable by default. Preserve the incident bundle/state evidence available in the current workflow, stop making unrelated state changes, and restart from a separately verified checkpoint or clean project state.

### Certificate verification failure

Treat the certificate as unauthenticated assurance evidence. Compare the expected artifact path/hash, retain the failed certificate for analysis, and regenerate a new certificate only from a known-good run state; do not overwrite the failed artifact if it may be needed for forensic comparison.

## 63.20 Reproducibility discipline

For a replayable assurance study, record at minimum:

- source revision and source-package hash;
- build type and relevant CMake options;
- platform/compiler/library versions;
- project/scenario/model hashes;
- random seeds;
- fault-campaign seed and manifest;
- checkpoint IDs/hashes;
- solver and precision configuration;
- conservation definitions/tolerances;
- numerical-evidence records;
- semantic dependency hashes;
- final run certificate.

A deterministic chaos seed alone is not enough if the command/evaluation sequence changes. Likewise, a matching cache key is not proof of physical validity; it means the semantic inputs/settings/dependencies encoded by the key are unchanged.

## 63.21 Performance and scaling considerations

The assurance framework is designed to keep expensive work selective:

- fault matching is scoped by subsystem/operation and deterministic rule state;
- checkpoint restore can be restricted to a hierarchical component scope;
- the semantic cache invalidates only entries that declare a changed dependency;
- `get_or_compute` avoids recomputation on a valid hit;
- conservation state is maintained per initialized domain/quantity rather than requiring a fixed global matrix;
- numerical evidence is stored as structured records and can be exported separately from high-rate telemetry.

For very large studies, define dependencies at useful engineering boundaries. A single dependency such as `entire-project` is easy to manage but causes broad invalidation. More specific dependencies such as `vehicle.geometry`, `tire.model`, `battery.calibration`, and `environment.weather` permit more useful incremental reuse.

## 63.22 Beginner and expert operating patterns

A beginner can use F7/Alt-M to discover assurance actions, view the generated command, press `Tab` to edit it, and execute through the same command dispatcher. This teaches the CLI rather than hiding it.

An expert can work entirely from the prompt or scripts. Recommended script behavior is to:

1. use canonical `industrial assurance ...` spellings;
2. create/verify a baseline checkpoint before a fault campaign;
3. set an explicit chaos seed;
4. fail the automation if checkpoint/certificate verification returns FAIL;
5. capture framework status before and after the run;
6. persist the final certificate alongside scientific results.

## 63.23 Testing and qualification

Configure and build the qualification targets:

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build build --target assurance_resilience_tests muzixdiagsys -j
```

Run focused assurance tests:

```bash
./build/assurance_resilience_tests
python3 tests/assurance_resilience_cli_regression.py ./build/muzixdiagsys .
```

Run the complete registered test matrix:

```bash
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
```

The assurance adversarial suite covers:

- deterministic probability replay;
- numeric corruption;
- production command dropping;
- malformed fault-manifest rejection;
- rollback after partial checkpoint mutation;
- hierarchical restore scope;
- restoration of real industrial signal state;
- causal error traces;
- balanced and unbalanced conservation closure;
- numerical trust classification and invalid-evidence rejection;
- semantic-cache hits, dependency invalidation, and recomputation;
- certificate creation, verification, and tamper detection.

The framework has also been exercised under focused AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and leak-detection qualification for the assurance paths.

## 63.24 Troubleshooting reference

| Symptom | Likely cause | Recommended action |
|---|---|---|
| Fault does not fire | Wrong subsystem/operation, wrong invocation count, once-rule already fired, rule disabled | Run `chaos status`, reset the campaign, verify the exact production operation name |
| Probability replay differs | Seed or evaluation sequence changed | Reproduce the same seed, rule set, and guarded-operation sequence |
| Corruption is followed by a normal validation error | Injected value violates the production signal/model contract | Confirm this is the intended fault; inspect corruption mode/value |
| Checkpoint restore reports rollback | A component restore callback failed | Inspect the returned error and error graph; verify checkpoint integrity |
| `ERR-ASSURANCE-RECOVERY` appears | Restore and clean rollback could not both complete | Preserve evidence and restart from a verified state |
| Conservation cell cannot accept a rate | Storage was never initialized | Set storage for that domain/quantity first |
| Conservation closes FAIL | Residual exceeds absolute-plus-relative tolerance | Check signs, units, transfers, missing storage, timing, and solver error |
| Numerical evidence is rejected | Invalid field, nonconvergence, out-of-domain state, or poor trust | Inspect `numerics get`, residual, condition, precision, uncertainty, and validity |
| Cache entry becomes stale after dependency update | Declared dependency hash changed | Recompute affected result or intentionally restore the prior dependency state |
| Cache file refuses to load | Dependency/key integrity mismatch or malformed schema | Treat the file as stale/corrupt; do not force-load it |
| Certificate verifies FAIL | Schema/digest/content mismatch | Preserve the failed artifact and regenerate only from known-good state |
| Menu action not desired | Beginner menu is optional | Press `Esc` and use the persistent CLI directly |

## 63.25 Qualification boundary and related documentation

SARR improves software assurance, reproducibility, and failure diagnosis; it does not certify the physical correctness of every model or prove that a real system satisfies legal or safety requirements. Conservation PASS means the configured ledger closed within the selected tolerances. Numerical `HIGH` means the evidence record satisfies the current trust policy. Certificate PASS means the authenticated manifest content matches its canonical SHA-256. Each result must still be interpreted in the context of model validity, experimental correlation, standards requirements, and qualified engineering review.

For implementation-level architecture and API details, see:

```text
docs/SIMULATION_ASSURANCE_RESILIENCE_REPRODUCIBILITY.md
SIMULATION_ASSURANCE_RESILIENCE_REPRODUCIBILITY_IMPLEMENTATION_REPORT_2026-08-07.md
SIMULATION_ASSURANCE_RESILIENCE_REPRODUCIBILITY_VALIDATION_2026-08-07.txt
```

# Chapter 64: Frontier Runtime, Positioning, and Sensing Platform

The Frontier Runtime, Positioning, and Sensing Platform is an additive research/HPC/navigation/sensor expansion. Its public API is `include/aesim/advanced/frontier_runtime_sensing_platform.hpp`, its dedicated qualification target is `frontier_runtime_sensing_platform_tests`, and its command family is `frontier-runtime`. It does not replace the existing SARR framework, distributed-execution services, numerical core, sensor models, advanced platform, or permanent command line. The new `frontier-runtime` command family routes through the existing advanced CLI dispatcher, and its public C++ services are exported by `aesim/advanced/platform.hpp`.

## 64.1 Build and discover capabilities

```bash
cmake -S . -B build/full -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DBUILD_TESTING=ON \
  -DAESIM_BUILD_TOOLS=ON
cmake --build build/full --target muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier_runtime_sensing_platform_tests -j
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime capabilities
```

The domains are:

```text
ulfm
checkpoint-compression
out-of-core
hardware-scheduler
floating-proof
lie-group
stiff-integrators
gnss-factor-graph
spad-lidar
coherent-lidar
radar-signature
```

General invocation:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform \
  frontier-runtime DOMAIN REQUEST.json OUTPUT.json [WORKING_DIRECTORY]
```

## 64.2 ULFM resilient distributed execution

`UlfmResilientRuntime` implements deterministic failed-rank membership, communicator generations, checkpoint integrity, survivor agreement semantics, mirrored rank state, and deterministic partition reassignment. A recovery advances the generation, removes failed ranks, assigns every partition to a survivor, selects a mirror survivor, verifies the SHA-256 of every recoverable failed-rank checkpoint, and emits an evidence SHA-256.

When the selected MPI implementation exports the User Level Failure Mitigation symbols `MPIX_Comm_revoke`, `MPIX_Comm_shrink`, and `MPIX_Comm_agree`, CMake defines `AESIM_HAVE_NATIVE_ULFM` and the recovery path can perform native communicator revocation, shrink, and agreement. If MPI/ULFM is not installed, the deterministic recovery engine remains fully operational for simulation, testing, scheduling, and failure studies. The capability document reports `native_ulfm_available`; the simulator does not claim native MPI repair when the symbols are absent.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform \
  frontier-runtime ulfm \
  examples/frontier_runtime/ulfm.json \
  build/results/ulfm.json
```

Important fields:

- `world_size`: original number of ranks.
- `partitions`: work partitions requiring ownership after recovery.
- `checkpoints[]`: `rank`, optional `mirror_rank`, and deterministic payload.
- `failed_ranks[]`: ranks to remove before recovery.

The result includes failed/surviving/recovered ranks, the new generation, partition owners/mirrors, native ULFM capability/attempt state, and evidence hash.

## 64.3 Error-bounded ZFP/SZ3 checkpoint compression

`ErrorBoundedCheckpointCompressor` implements two deterministic error-bounded checkpoint profiles:

- `zfp-fixed-accuracy`: fixed-accuracy scalar quantization with signed variable-length coding.
- `sz3-predictive`: the same strict error contract with predictive delta coding between quantized samples.

For a requested absolute error bound `E`, the quantization step is at most `2E`, so nearest-integer reconstruction has an ideal quantization error no larger than `E`; verification includes floating-point slack. If a positive relative bound is also requested, the compressor chooses a global step constrained by the smallest nonzero magnitude so both contracts can be checked.

The persisted `.mzcp` format contains codec identity, element count, absolute/relative bounds, quantization step, payload length, and payload. Payload SHA-256 is verified before decompression. Truncated files, invalid codec IDs, malformed variable-length integers, integer overflow, and trailing data are rejected.

The built-in codecs are complete MuzixDiagSys checkpoint formats. They are intentionally **not described as third-party ZFP or SZ3 bitstreams**. Native external-library adapters may be added when those libraries are available without changing the public checkpoint contract.

Examples:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime checkpoint-compression \
  examples/frontier_runtime/checkpoint_zfp.json build/results/zfp.json build/results/zfp-work

./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime checkpoint-compression \
  examples/frontier_runtime/checkpoint_sz3.json build/results/sz3.json build/results/sz3-work
```

The result reports compression ratio, payload size/hash, maximum observed absolute/relative error, and PASS/FAIL against the requested contract.

## 64.4 Out-of-core simulation arrays

`OutOfCoreArray` exposes a persistent binary64 array whose chunks are demand-paged from a backing file. The cache is bounded by `max_resident_chunks` and uses LRU eviction. Dirty chunks are written before eviction and on `flush()`/destruction. Reopening validates the exact expected file size.

Runtime statistics include:

- cache hits and misses;
- evictions;
- dirty flushes;
- current resident chunk count;
- chunk size and element count;
- optional SHA-256 of the fully flushed backing file.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime out-of-core \
  examples/frontier_runtime/out_of_core.json build/results/ooc.json build/results/ooc-work
```

Use this layer for state vectors, field tiles, ensemble buffers, long histories, and intermediate arrays that must exceed a configured in-memory working set without changing numerical values.

## 64.5 Hardware-aware runtime scheduler

`HardwareAwareScheduler::discover()` inventories logical CPUs, physical CPU packages, Linux NUMA nodes, node CPU lists, node memory capacity, DRM GPU devices, PCI addresses, and GPU NUMA locality where the OS exposes them. Other operating systems retain a portable single-node fallback.

`place()` selects a NUMA node that satisfies requested CPU threads, memory, optional GPU requirement, and optional preferred node. `apply_cpu_affinity()` uses Linux `sched_setaffinity` and returns an explicit error on unsupported systems or invalid CPU IDs.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime hardware-scheduler \
  examples/frontier_runtime/hardware_scheduler.json build/results/hardware.json
```

A missing GPU is a real infeasible placement when `require_gpu=true`; it is never silently substituted with a CPU.

## 64.6 Formal floating-point verification certificates

`FloatingPointVerifier` emits machine-checkable binary64 error certificates for:

- sequential summation;
- sequential dot products;
- Horner polynomial evaluation.

The certificates use the standard unit roundoff `u = epsilon/2` and a Higham-style `gamma_n = nu/(1-nu)` forward-error envelope. Reference values are accumulated in extended precision. Every certificate includes operation type/count, binary64 result, extended reference, observed error, certified bound, assumptions, PASS/FAIL, and SHA-256 over the certificate evidence.

This is a formal arithmetic error-bound certificate under its stated IEEE-754 assumptions. It does not prove the correctness of a physical model or algorithmic specification.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime floating-proof \
  examples/frontier_runtime/floating_proof.json build/results/floating-proof.json
```

Supported operations are `sum`, `dot`, and `horner`.

## 64.7 Lie-group and variational integrators

### 64.7.1 SO(3) rigid-body integration

`LieGroupIntegrator` evolves orientation using a quaternion exponential-map increment derived from the midpoint angular velocity. Body angular acceleration uses Euler rigid-body equations with principal inertias and applied torque. Every orientation update is normalized and validated.

The method avoids integrating quaternion components as unrelated Euclidean states and is intended for rigid-body attitude, wheel/sensor frames, multibody orientation blocks, and long-running rotational simulations.

### 64.7.2 Störmer-Verlet variational integration

`VariationalIntegrator::stormer_verlet()` performs momentum half-step, position drift, and final momentum half-step for separable Hamiltonian systems. It is time-reversible and symplectic for the documented problem class.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime lie-group \
  examples/frontier_runtime/lie_group.json build/results/lie-group.json
```

The command reports maximum quaternion norm deviation and maximum oscillator energy deviation during the requested integration.

## 64.8 Radau IIA, Rosenbrock-W, and IMEX integration

`StiffIntegrator` provides three general vector ODE families using `aesim::core::numerics` for stable Jacobians and linear solves:

### Radau IIA

The implementation is the two-stage, third-order Radau IIA collocation formula. Both stages are solved simultaneously with Newton iterations. The block Newton matrix contains finite-difference Jacobians evaluated at each collocation state. Failed linear solves or nonlinear convergence return a non-converged result rather than silently accepting a step.

### Rosenbrock-W

The Rosenbrock-W1 path forms a numerical Jacobian and solves the linearly implicit system `(I - hJ) k = f`, then advances `y += hk`. This is a robust first-order L-stable linearly implicit step for stiff decay and as a baseline member of the Rosenbrock family.

### IMEX

The IMEX path uses an explicit Heun predictor/corrector contribution combined with an implicit trapezoidal contribution. The implicit state is solved with Newton iterations and a numerical Jacobian of only the implicit partition.

Examples:

```bash
for method in radau rosenbrock-w imex; do
  ./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime stiff-integrators \
    examples/frontier_runtime/stiff_${method//-/_}.json \
    build/results/stiff-${method}.json
done
```

Result evidence includes method, final time/state, step count, nonlinear iterations, final residual, convergence, and a reference result for the built-in linear-decay CLI problem.

## 64.9 Full GNSS carrier-phase and factor-graph stack

`GnssCarrierPhaseFactorGraph` supports:

- Standalone, PPP, RTK, and PPP-RTK modes;
- pseudorange, carrier phase, and Doppler observations;
- dual-frequency ionosphere-free code and carrier combinations;
- satellite clock bias/drift corrections;
- ionosphere, troposphere mapping, code bias, phase bias, phase windup, and relativistic corrections;
- base-station differencing for RTK-family modes;
- floating carrier ambiguities and deterministic integer candidate/ratio testing;
- explicit cycle-slip ambiguity segmentation;
- sliding-window operation;
- nine navigation states per epoch: ECEF position (3), receiver clock bias, ECEF velocity (3), clock drift, and zenith-wet troposphere state;
- constant-velocity, clock, and troposphere process factors;
- IMU delta-position/delta-velocity preintegration factors;
- wheel-speed factors;
- map-position constraints;
- QR-based weighted least squares using the hardened numerical core;
- code, carrier, and Doppler RMS qualification metrics;
- SHA-256 evidence identity.

### Sign conventions

The carrier measurement supplied to the API is phase in cycles and a positive wavelength. Doppler is converted to observed range rate as `-doppler_hz * wavelength_m`. Satellite clock fields are expressed as range-equivalent meters or meters/second. Position/velocity are ECEF meters and meters/second.

### Dual-frequency combination

For frequencies `f1` and `f2`, code and carrier meters use:

```text
X_IF = (f1^2 X1 - f2^2 X2) / (f1^2 - f2^2)
```

The explicit ionosphere term is then zero in the combined measurement model.

### RTK-family base fields

Set `has_base=true` and provide `base_position_m`, `base_pseudorange_m`, and `base_carrier_phase_cycles`. The runtime removes the base measurement-minus-geometric-range common component before the rover factor is formed.

### Integer ambiguity ratio

Floating ambiguity meters are mapped to cycles using the measurement wavelength. The nearest integer candidate is the best candidate and the nearest alternative is used to construct a deterministic second/best squared-distance ratio. Integer results are reported only when the configured threshold is satisfied.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime gnss-factor-graph \
  examples/frontier_runtime/gnss_factor_graph.json build/results/gnss.json
```

The canonical example includes multi-epoch receiver motion, dual-frequency PPP, satellite clock/drift, IMU preintegration, wheel speed, and map factors.

## 64.10 SPAD photon-counting LiDAR

`SpadLidarSimulator` models:

- Poisson signal photons;
- photon-detection efficiency;
- background and dark-count Poisson processes;
- Gaussian timing jitter;
- detector dead time and suppressed-event accounting;
- finite histogram bins and observation window;
- two-way time-of-flight range estimation;
- deterministic random seeding.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime spad-lidar \
  examples/frontier_runtime/spad_lidar.json build/results/spad.json
```

The returned histogram is the accepted-detector histogram after dead-time suppression, not an ideal photon-arrival histogram.

## 64.11 Coherent FMCW LiDAR

`CoherentLidarSimulator` synthesizes noisy complex up/down chirp beat signals. The ideal beat pair is:

```text
f_up   = S tau + f_d
f_down = S tau - f_d
```

where `S` is chirp slope, `tau=2R/c`, and `f_d=2v/lambda`. The estimator derives beat frequency from complex adjacent-sample phase correlation and unwraps it around the known physical band. Range and velocity are recovered jointly:

```text
R = c (f_up + f_down) / (4 S)
v = lambda (f_up - f_down) / 4
```

Noise is complex Gaussian with amplitude determined by `snr_db` and deterministic `seed`.

## 64.12 Radar micro-Doppler and polarimetry

`RadarSignatureSimulator` builds coherent slow-time returns from multiple scatterers. Each scatterer may contain bulk radial velocity plus sinusoidal micro-velocity, which is analytically integrated into displacement before phase modulation. A deterministic DFT produces Doppler power, and the strongest bins are returned with radial-velocity conversion.

Polarimetry accepts complex HH/HV/VH/VV values represented as `[real, imag]`. The result contains cross-pol/co-pol ratios and three Pauli-basis powers. A SHA-256 identifies the result evidence.

Example:

```bash
./build/full/muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform frontier-runtime radar-signature \
  examples/frontier_runtime/radar_signature.json build/results/radar.json
```

## 64.14 Compatibility and engineering boundaries

- Existing public APIs and CLI families remain available.
- `frontier-runtime` is additive to `muzixdiagsys_advanced_platform`.
- Native ULFM is used only when the MPI implementation actually exposes the MPIX functions; otherwise capability state is explicit.
- The built-in ZFP/SZ3 profiles are complete deterministic MuzixDiagSys codecs with strict error contracts, not counterfeit external bitstreams.
- Hardware discovery depends on information exposed by the host OS; missing GPU/NUMA data remains explicit.
- Floating-point certificates prove only the documented arithmetic error envelope under their assumptions.
- GNSS, LiDAR, and radar outputs are simulation/engineering evidence and require external measurement correlation before physical qualification claims.

## 65.1 Implemented domains

The current platform provides all of the following operational domains:

1. `safe-reinforcement-learning-laboratory`: deterministic constrained policy learning against the vector vehicle environment, seeded population search, safety costs, lane/proximity invariant shielding, policy evidence, and invalid-dimension rejection.
2. `asam-cmp-capture-platform`: deterministic CMP-oriented capture, binary encoding/decoding, CRC32, timestamps and sequencing, duplicate/reorder/gap accounting, corruption rejection, and persistent archives.
3. `asam-traffic-participants-platform`: normalized passenger-car, truck, bus, motorcycle, bicycle, pedestrian, trailer, emergency-vehicle, and other participant definitions with schema validation and OpenSCENARIO/OSI-style mappings.
4. `sysml-v2-repository-integration`: local content-addressed repository with immutable commits, parents, branches, preserved element identities, SHA-256 identifiers, queries, and diffs.
5. `scientific-streaming-io-platform`: append-only zlib-compressed, length-delimited, CRC-protected scientific records with replay, time/variable filtering, truncation detection, and file SHA-256.
6. `modern-mpi-transport-runtime`: deterministic partitioning/reduction plus persistent collective and MPI Session functionality when supported by the actual MPI installation; serial operation remains explicit when MPI is absent.
7. `qualified-external-solver-backends`: native LU, CG, BiCGSTAB, independently recomputed residuals, cross-solver consensus, and a shell-free external linear-solver process protocol.
8. `automotive-sensor-bus-physical-layer`: SENT, PSI5, DSI3, and CXPI waveform generation/decoding, checksums/parity, timing, jitter, edge-loss faults, bitrate evidence, and round-trip qualification.
9. `materialx-gltf-asset-pipeline`: glTF 2.0 and MaterialX 1.38 PBR material interchange with IOR, transmission, engineering LiDAR reflectivity, and radar permittivity/loss-tangent data.
10. `gpu-particle-multiphysics-runtime`: deterministic host SPH and DEM with spatial hashing and optional capability-gated HIP execution.
11. `lubricant-chemistry-condition-monitoring`: oxidation, nitration, additive reserve, soot, water, fuel dilution, TAN/TBN, viscosity, wear-metal and varnish evolution with service-state classification.
12. `tire-acoustic-and-uniformity-laboratory`: rotational/cavity/tread frequencies, harmonics, acoustic level, radial/lateral force variation, conicity, ply steer, imbalance, flat spotting, and uniformity score.
13. `hazop-bowtie-barrier-assurance`: HAZOP guidewords, causes/consequences, prevention/mitigation barriers, common-cause beta effects, event trees, and frequency propagation.
14. `software-supply-chain-evidence-platform`: SPDX-oriented component records, VEX dispositions, SARIF-oriented findings, CVSS/license release gates, reproducibility checks, and cryptographic evidence.
